title: The Built Environment and Spatial Form
research_question: To define major areas of research, critically evaluate contributions, and suggest future directions in the study of the built environment and spatial form, focusing on how built forms accommodate human behavior, express culture, relate to the self, and are produced/reproduced by society.

findings.antecedent: Built forms (size, shape, internal configuration, materials)
findings.consequent: Accommodation of human behavior, adaptation to needs, reflection of social organization (e.g., household size, residence practices)
findings.mechanism: Human groups seek to adapt their buildings to behavioral and functional needs; when fit is lacking, construction, renovation, or relocation occurs, or behavior changes to fit the environment.
findings.quote: human groups seek to adapt their buildings to their behavioral needs or functional requirements

findings.antecedent: Built forms (configuration, content, associations, site plans, architectural elements)
findings.consequent: Expression/representation of social/political structures, cultural identity, cosmological meanings, values
findings.mechanism: Built forms act as communicative and mnemonic devices, condensing powerful meanings and values, manipulated by actors, and embodying ideal conceptions of social, political, and religious life.
findings.quote: Built forms and site plans act as communicative or mnemonic devices expressing or reaffirming through symbolic associations relations between groups

findings.antecedent: Built environment (house as symbol, spatial configurations, 'carpentered' world, personal space)
findings.consequent: Conceptions of the self, spatial perception, orientation, psychological development, social interaction patterns (e.g., privacy, crowding, territoriality)
findings.mechanism: Symbols in the built environment represent latent thoughts or universal archetypes; spatial schemas are basic to human orientation; culture modifies innate distancing mechanisms (personal space); built forms enable or constrain behaviors.
findings.quote: The house as a fundamental symbol, as well as protector, of the self.

findings.antecedent: Social, political, and economic forces (e.g., class, gender, race relations, capital accumulation, planning policies, power structures)
findings.consequent: Production and reproduction of built forms (urban planning, colonial settlements, housing types), social action, maintenance/reinforcement of social forms/ideologies
findings.mechanism: Built forms are social and cultural products, accommodating functions and governed by societal ideas; they are produced through macrolevel planning and decision-making, often serving ideological ends of dominant classes.
findings.quote: Theories of the social production of built form focus on the social, political, and economic forces that produce the built environment, and conversely, the impact of the socially produced built environment on social action.

mechanisms: Human groups adapt buildings to behavioral and functional needs; when fit is lacking, construction, renovation, or relocation occurs, or behavior changes to fit the environment.
Built forms act as communicative and mnemonic devices, condensing powerful meanings and values, manipulated by actors, and embodying ideal conceptions of social, political, and religious life.

Symbols in the built environment represent latent thoughts or universal archetypes; spatial schemas are basic to human orientation; culture modifies innate distancing mechanisms (personal space); built forms enable or constrain behaviors.

Built forms are social and cultural products, accommodating functions and governed by societal ideas; they are produced through macrolevel planning and decision-making, often serving ideological ends of dominant classes.
implementation_implications: Anthropologists should examine how architectural researchers document and describe built forms (e.g., axonometric drawing) for new ways to view, recall, and analyze the built environment.
Exploring theories of the physical environment focusing on metaphor or designed architectural forms/urban plans can foster collaboration between anthropologists and design professionals.
Continued research in social organization and symbolism is essential, providing a base for better theoretical development in social production.

Systematic documentation and analysis of physical attributes of the built environment will benefit from better systematic analyses of household cultural processes, potentially using a decision-making approach.
limitations: Theoretical development and empirical work across the major research areas (accommodation, meaning, self-relation, social production) are uneven.
The processes by which decisions are made to build, remodel, or move are not well documented or understood in most societies where anthropologists have worked.
The meaning of the built environment as revealed through metaphorical connections and ritual practices is an incompletely explored dimension.

Existing approaches are not perfectly adequate on their own; building decisions cannot be understood apart from social/economic institutional forces, nor can symbolic meaning be divorced from these forces or history.

paper_metadata.title: A case study on the effect of light and colors in the built environment on autistic children’s behavior
paper_metadata.crossref_title: A case study on the effect of light and colors in the built environment on autistic children’s behavior
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: BackgroundThe importance of strategies and services by caregivers and family members substantially impact the psychological and emotional wellbeing of autistic children. The rapid research developments in clinical and non-clinical methods benefit the features of autistic children. Among various internal and external factors, the influence of the built environment also impacts the characteristics of autistic children. This study investigates primarily the psychological effect of light and colors on the mood and behavior of autistic children to identify the most favorable and preferred indoor lights and color shades.MethodsA questionnaire survey was conducted at an autism center among autistic children and their parents. This study included autistic children aged between 6 and 16 (45 males, 42 females, mean age 8.7 years, standard deviation 2.3). Eighty-seven participants were involved in the survey to determine the sensory perceptions, intolerance, preferences, and sensitivities of children with an autism spectrum disorder toward colors and lighting. The margin of error at the statistical analysis’s 95% confidence level is ± 0.481.ResultsAs per this case report, the children have various color preferences and respond differently to different shades. Different hues have varying effects on autistic children, with many neutral tones and mellow shades proven to be autistic-friendly with their calming and soothing effect, while bright, bold, and intense colors are refreshing and stimulating. The stimulus of bright-lighting causes behavioral changes in autistic children prone to light sensitivity.ConclusionThe insights gained from this interaction with parents and caretakers of autistic children could be helpful for designers to incorporate specific autistic-friendly design elements that make productive interior spaces. A complete understanding of the effect of factors like color and lighting on the learning ability and engagement of autistic children in an indoor environment is essential for designers and clinicians. The main findings of this study could be helpful for a designer and clinicians to address designing an autism-friendly built environment with a color palette and lighting scheme conducive to their wellbeing and to maximize their cognitive functioning.
